title: AIXI
subtitle: Universal artificial intelligence: induction, planning and the limits of the ideal agent
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A 12-chapter course on AIXI, Marcus Hutter's mathematical definition of an ideal reinforcement learning agent. Based on Hutter's Universal Algorithmic Intelligence survey, the Monte-Carlo AIXI paper by Veness and colleagues, Legg and Hutter's universal intelligence paper, and Leike, Hutter and Orseau on computability and bad priors. Covers the agent-environment cycle, expectimax, Bayesian mixtures, Kolmogorov complexity, Solomonoff induction, the AIXI equation, horizons, optimality, incomputability and AIXItl, MC-AIXI-CTW and critiques. Python labs run on the built-in MicroPython engine. The toy programs are teaching miniatures, not code from the papers.

chapters.title: What is AIXI?

maps.title: The big picture
links: AIXI | is | A reinforcement learning agent

summary: AIXI is a mathematical definition of an ideal reinforcement learning agent, proposed by Marcus Hutter in 2000. It is not a program you can run. It answers a thought experiment: how would you act if you had unlimited computing power and no knowledge of your world?

It joins two ideas. Solomonoff induction predicts what comes next by weighing every computable explanation of the past, simple ones more heavily. Expectimax planning then picks the action with the highest expected total reward under those predictions.
The course builds both halves in small Python programs, then the real approximations and the serious criticisms.

glossary.def: Hutter's universal reinforcement learning agent: Solomonoff prediction plus expectimax planning. Pronounced eye-ksee.
Whatever chooses actions: it reads percepts and writes actions.
Everything outside the agent; it answers each action with a percept.
What the agent receives each step: an observation and a reward.
Prediction that mixes all computable hypotheses, weighted by 2 to the minus program length.
Planning that maximizes over your actions and averages over the environment's replies.
Cannot be computed by any program, even given unlimited time.

keyPoints: AIXI was proposed by Marcus Hutter in 2000; the main results are in his 2005 book Universal Artificial Intelligence.
It acts in an unknown but computable environment and tries to maximize total reward.
Prediction comes from a Solomonoff-style mixture; action comes from expectimax.
There are no free parameters except the choice of universal Turing machine and the horizon.
AIXI is incomputable, so it is a gold standard to approximate, not a program to run.
It does not model itself as part of the world: that is its biggest conceptual limit.

items: Explain it simply. AIXI is a thought experiment: the smartest possible player of any game, if it had unlimited time. Like a chess grandmaster who tries every future in their head, but for all of life. We can never build it, yet it shows what perfect learning would look like.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does AIXI combine, and why can it never be built?

Intelligence is hard to define, and harder to define for machines unlike us. Marcus Hutter's answer, published first in 2000 and developed in his 2005 book, takes the problem from the top down: instead of building a clever system and hoping it is general, define the best possible agent mathematically, then ask how closely it can be approximated.

The setting is the general reinforcement learning problem. An agent and an environment talk in cycles. Each cycle the agent sends an action, and the environment replies with a percept made of an observation and a reward.
The agent wants as much total reward as it can get, and it knows nothing about the environment except that some computer program could produce its replies.

AIXI has two halves. The first half is learning. Following Ray Solomonoff's 1964 theory of induction, it keeps every computable explanation of its experience, and trusts each in proportion to two to the power of minus the length of the shortest program that states it.
Short explanations count for much more, a formal version of Occam's razor.

The second half is acting. Given its beliefs, AIXI looks ahead over all its possible action sequences and the environment's possible replies, and takes the action whose average future reward is highest.
This look-ahead is called expectimax, because it takes a maximum over the agent's choices and an expectation over the environment's chance.

What do we get? Hutter's analysis argues that the result is optimal in several senses, which chapter 9 lists, and chapter 12 shows how later work weakened several of those claims. The agent also has a price: it must consider all programs, including ones that never halt, so it cannot be computed.

Do not read AIXI as a design to build. Read it as a yardstick, like the ideal gas or the frictionless plane. It tells you what perfect general learning would be, which parts of that are hopeless for finite machines, and which approximations keep something of the spirit.
The Monte Carlo AIXI work of Veness and colleagues, chapter 11, is the best known attempt.

A note on sources. This course follows Hutter's 2007 survey Universal Algorithmic Intelligence, the Veness and colleagues 2011 paper in the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, Legg and Hutter's universal intelligence paper, and papers by Leike and Hutter and by Orseau on the weaknesses.
The toy programs are my own teaching examples, not code from those papers.

summary: The formal setting is simple. Time runs in steps. At step t the agent picks an action a_t from a finite set and the environment replies with a percept, an observation o_t and a reward r_t. Everything seen so far is the history.

A policy maps each history to an action. An environment maps each history and action to a distribution over percepts. There is no assumption that the world is Markov: the reply may depend on the whole past.

The environment must be chronological: its reply at step t cannot depend on actions the agent has not taken yet. This sounds obvious but needs stating when everything is written as functions on strings.

keyPoints: A step is an action followed by a percept (observation, reward).
A history is the list of all action-percept pairs so far.
A policy turns a history into an action; an environment turns a history and action into a percept distribution.

items: Explain it simply. Think of a ping-pong game. You act, the world answers, you act again. The agent sends an action and gets back a picture of the world plus a reward. Every learner, from a baby to a robot, runs this loop.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what are the three things exchanged in each cycle?

Start with the vocabulary of the framework in Hutter's survey. There is a finite set of possible actions, a finite set of observations and a set of rewards, usually numbers between zero and one. In cycle k the agent outputs an action.
The environment then produces a percept, which carries both an observation and a reward. Then cycle k plus one begins.

The history after k cycles is the list of all actions and percepts so far, in order. It is everything the agent has ever experienced. A policy is a function from histories to actions. The agent's whole behaviour is its policy, so comparing agents means comparing policies.

The environment is also a function of the history. In the deterministic case the next percept is a fixed function of the actions so far. In general it is a probability distribution over percepts, given the history and the action just taken.

Veness and colleagues define an environment as a sequence of conditional probability functions that obey one consistency condition, that actions do not affect earlier percepts. Hutter calls such environments chronological.

Read this as the probability that the environment nu produces percept x at step t, given all earlier actions and percepts and the action just taken. Nothing says the world has a hidden state with the Markov property.
A single unseen switch that was flipped fifty steps ago may still matter, and that is allowed.

This generality is the point. Many problems that look different fit the same mould. A game against an opponent, a sequence to predict, a function to minimize or a supervised learning task can each be written as an environment with the right observations and rewards.
Hutter's survey lists exactly these classes, and a chapter of his book is devoted to showing how each one fits.

The goal is stated through the reward. The agent wants to maximize the sum of rewards over a horizon m, the number of cycles it plans for. Chapter 8 returns to how the horizon is chosen. For now treat it as a fixed number of future steps.
The practice section builds a small deterministic environment with memory, so you can see how the reply depends on the history. You then run a policy in it and add up the reward.

practice.title: An environment with memory
practice.intro: Write env_reply(actions): given the list of all actions so far (the last one is the current action, each 0 or 1), return [obs, reward]. obs is 1 if the number of 1s among the actions so far is odd, otherwise 0. reward is 1 if the current action equals the previous observation (the observation from the step before; before the first step it is 0), otherwise 0.
practice.hint: The previous observation is the parity of all actions except the last.
practice.solution:
def env_reply(actions):
    prev_obs = sum(actions[:-1]) % 2
    obs = sum(actions) % 2
    reward = 0
    if actions[-1] == prev_obs:
        reward = 1
    return [obs, reward]

practice.title: Run a policy
practice.intro: Using the same environment (obs is the parity of the number of 1s among actions so far; reward is 1 when the current action equals the previous observation, which starts at 0), write total_reward(steps): the agent plays 'copy the last observation' (its first action is 0, afterwards it plays the most recent observation). Return the total reward over steps steps.
practice.hint: Keep the action list; compute the parity before and after adding the new action.
practice.solution:
def total_reward(steps):
    actions = []
    last_obs = 0
    total = 0
    for t in range(steps):
        a = last_obs
        actions.append(a)
        prev_obs = sum(actions[:-1]) % 2
        obs = sum(actions) % 2
        if a == prev_obs:
            total += 1
        last_obs = obs
    return total

chapters.title: Planning with a known model: expectimax

maps.title: Expectimax
links: Tree size | grows | Exponentially with horizon

summary: Suppose the agent knows the environment exactly. Then choosing actions is a planning problem. Draw a tree: at agent nodes pick the best action, at chance nodes average over the environment's replies, and add up rewards along the way. This is expectimax.

The value of a history is the expected total reward the best policy can still collect. The recursion is: value is the maximum over actions of the expected, over percepts, of reward plus the value of the longer history.
The tree grows exponentially with the horizon, which is the first reason AIXI cannot be run. The second is that the environment is not known, which is where Solomonoff induction comes in.

glossary.def: Game-tree search with max nodes for the agent and expectation nodes for chance.
The expected total future reward under a policy or the best policy.
A policy that attains the highest value.
The recursion value = max over actions of the expectation of reward plus next value.
The number of future steps counted.
A node where the environment draws the next percept.

keyPoints: With a known environment, optimal action is a search problem.
Max over actions, expectation over percepts, sum of rewards.
V(h) = max_a sum_x P(x | h a) [ r(x) + V(h a x) ] with V = 0 at the horizon.
The search tree has (actions x percepts)^horizon leaves.
AIXI uses this same recursion, with the true environment replaced by a mixture.
Sampling approximations such as UCT avoid expanding the whole tree.

items: Explain it simply. Planning with a known model is like playing chess in your head when you know every rule. You imagine each move, each reply, each next move, and pick the path with the best average score. Expectimax does this with a tree.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: how does expectimax choose between actions and average over outcomes?
Forget learning for a chapter. Assume the agent is told the exact environment, meaning a rule that gives the probability of each percept after each history and action.
What should it do? This is a decision problem under uncertainty, and the classical solution is dynamic programming, the Bellman equation.

Define the value of a history h with k steps left as the expected total reward from now on, if the agent plays the best possible way. With no steps left the value is zero. With steps left, try each action a. For each, the environment answers with percept x with some probability.
The percept brings reward r and a longer history. Average reward plus future value over the percepts, then pick the action with the highest average.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} V_k(h) \;=\; \max_{a}\; \sum_{x} P(x \mid h, a)\,\bigl[\, r(x) + V_{k-1}(h\,a\,x)\,\bigr], \\[0.6em] V_0 = 0 \end{gathered}

items: Written as a tree, the actions form max nodes and the percepts form chance nodes, stacked alternately. The leaves are at depth k. The number of leaves is the number of actions times the number of percepts, raised to the power k.
A binary action, a binary reward and a horizon of twenty already give about a trillion leaves, which is why exact planning only works for small cases.

Two observations will matter later. First, an optimal policy exists for every finite horizon and can be found by the backward recursion above. Second, because the environment's replies can depend on the full history, the tree must be indexed by histories, not by states.
AIXI uses exactly this recursion. The only change is that the true probabilities are replaced by a mixture, the subject of the next chapters.

Veness and colleagues note that expectimax cannot be done exactly at scale and use a Monte Carlo tree search instead, in a version of the UCT algorithm they call rho-UCT. It samples trajectories through the tree and spends more effort on promising branches. Chapter 11 sets out how it works.
In the practice section you evaluate small expectimax trees, then plan in a stochastic environment whose reward chances depend on the previous action.

chapters.title: Bayesian mixtures and prediction

maps.title: Mixtures
links: Bayes rule | updates | Weights by likelihood
Dominance | bounds | Loss by log of 1 over weight

summary: When the environment is unknown, a Bayesian keeps several candidates, each with a prior weight. As data arrives, candidates that predicted it badly lose weight. To predict, average the candidates' predictions using the current weights.

The mixture has a remarkable property. It assigns every observed sequence at least its prior weight times the probability that the true candidate gave it. So it can never do much worse than the best candidate, and the extra cost is at most the log of one over that candidate's weight.
AIXI uses the largest sensible class, all computable environments, and a particular prior, which is the topic of the next chapters.

glossary.def: The set of environments the agent considers possible.
Weights on hypotheses before seeing data; they sum to at most one.
Weights after seeing data, by Bayes rule.
A weighted average of the hypotheses' probabilities; written xi.
xi(x) is at least w times nu(x) for every member nu with weight w.
The probability a hypothesis gave to the data actually seen.

keyPoints: Bayes rule: new weight is proportional to old weight times likelihood.
Mixture probability xi(x) = sum of w_i times nu_i(x).
Dominance: xi(x) >= w_i nu_i(x) for each i.
Hence the log-loss of the mixture exceeds the best member's by at most ln(1/w_i).
For deterministic hypotheses, the mixture's mistakes are bounded by the log of one over the true hypothesis's weight in bits.
A class containing the truth with positive prior weight is called a grain of truth.

items: Explain it simply. Imagine many friends each guessing what happens next. You trust each in proportion to how well they have done so far. A Bayesian mixture is that crowd, and its vote is never much worse than its best friend.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why is a mixture never much worse than its best member?

A hypothesis here is a complete probabilistic model of the environment: given a history it says how likely each next percept is. Suppose the agent has a list of such models, nu one, nu two and so on, and a prior weight for each, w one, w two, adding up to at most one. How should it predict?

The Bayesian mixture is the answer. The agent's probability of any data x is the weighted sum of the models' probabilities. Written as an equation, xi of x equals the sum over i of w i times nu i of x. It is a legitimate probability model in its own right.

Bayes rule updates the weights. After seeing x, the posterior weight of model i is its old weight times the probability it gave to x, divided by the mixture's probability of x. A model that predicted x well gains weight. A model that gave x probability zero loses all weight and never returns.
Predicting the next symbol means averaging the models' next-symbol predictions with these posterior weights.

Now the key inequality. Because the mixture is a sum of non-negative terms, it is at least each single term. So xi of x is at least w i times nu i of x, for every member i. Taking logarithms, the mixture's log-loss on the data exceeds the log-loss of model i by at most the log of one over w i.
This holds for any data, whatever the truth.

If the data really is drawn from model i, the mixture's total loss exceeds the best possible by a constant that depends only on the prior weight of the truth, not on how long the data goes on. A good prior weight is therefore a bounded one-time cost.
Solomonoff chose weights so that every computable model gets a decent share, and the next chapters show how.

There is a catch that foreshadows chapter 12. Dominance only helps when the truth is in the class with positive weight, the so-called grain of truth. And in the agent setting, the data depends on what the agent does, so a mixture that predicts passively well may still act badly.
The practice section implements Bayes updating, the mixture prediction and the regret bound for coin-flip hypotheses.

chapters.title: Kolmogorov complexity and the universal prior

maps.title: Complexity
links: Kolmogorov complexity | is | Length of shortest program
Invariance theorem | bounds | Change of machine
Universal prior | weights | 2 to minus length
Occam | is formalized by | Short programs

summary: The Kolmogorov complexity of a string is the length of the shortest program that prints it on a fixed universal computer. A string with a pattern has a short program. A random string has no program much shorter than itself.
Changing the computer changes the complexity by at most a constant, so the notion is meaningful. But no program can compute it exactly.
The universal prior gives a string the total weight of all programs that produce it, each program counting two to the power of minus its length. This is Occam's razor written as arithmetic.

glossary.def: K(x): the length of the shortest program that outputs x on a given universal machine.
A machine that can simulate any other machine given its description as part of the program.
For two universal machines, complexities differ by at most a constant not depending on x.
No program is the beginning of another program.
For a prefix-free set of programs, the sum of 2^-length is at most 1.
Probability of a string = sum of 2^-length over programs that produce it.
No algorithm computes K(x) for every x.

keyPoints: K(x) is the length of the shortest program printing x.
The reference machine matters only up to an additive constant (invariance theorem).
K is not computable.
Prefix-free programs obey the Kraft inequality, so 2^-length can be read as probabilities.
M(x) is the sum of 2^-length(p) over programs whose output starts with x.
Shorter explanations get exponentially more weight.

items: Explain it simply. The shortest instructions that make a computer print something measure how complicated it is. A page of repeating dots is simple; random noise is not. The universal prior says: shorter explanations are more likely.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what is Kolmogorov complexity and why prefer short programs?

Compare two strings of a thousand bits. The first is zero, one, zero, one, and so on. The second is the result of a thousand fair coin flips. The first can be described by a very short program: print zero one, five hundred times. The second seems to need a program that contains the bits themselves.
Kolmogorov complexity makes this precise.

Fix a universal computer U. The Kolmogorov complexity of a string x, written K of x, is the length in bits of the shortest program that makes U print x. Solomonoff, Kolmogorov and Chaitin each arrived at this idea independently in the 1960s.
A string is regular when K of x is much smaller than its length.

Which computer? The invariance theorem says it hardly matters for long strings. If V is another universal computer, then K under U and K under V differ by at most a constant c that depends on U and V but not on the string, because U can simulate V given a fixed-length interpreter.
Chapter 12 returns to this: the constant is harmless in theory, yet for the short histories an agent sees in practice it can matter a lot.

Kolmogorov complexity cannot be computed. If a program could compute K, we could use it to search for the first string whose complexity exceeds some large number n, but that search would itself be a short program, only about log n bits long, which is a contradiction.
We can compute upper bounds, by finding some program, and never prove that a bound is tight in general.

Now turn lengths into probabilities. Take programs to be bit strings from a prefix-free set: no program is the beginning of another. A fair coin that produces bits one at a time and stops when a complete program has appeared gives program p probability two to the power of minus its length.
The Kraft inequality guarantees that these probabilities add up to at most one.

This is Solomonoff's universal prior, in the monotone form used for prediction. The probability of a string x is the chance that U, fed with random bits, prints something that begins with x. Strings with short programs get large probability.
A string with complexity K gets probability roughly two to the minus K, up to terms of lower order, so a string with a program ten bits shorter is a thousand times more likely.

The practice section uses a toy machine, my own illustration. A program is n ones, then a zero, then a pattern of exactly n bits; the machine repeats the pattern forever. The program length is two n plus one.
You can run it, compute the shortest program for a string, check that the set is prefix-free and compute the prior over a finite set of programs.

maps.title: Universal prediction
links: Solomonoff prior | is | A mixture of all computable measures

Dominance constant | is | 2 to minus K of mu

summary: Solomonoff induction predicts the next symbol by the ratio M of x followed by a symbol, to M of x. It is the Bayesian mixture of chapter 4 over every computable hypothesis, with weights from the universal prior.

Its signature result is a bound on total error. If the data comes from any computable source mu, the predictions converge to mu's own, and the total prediction error, however long the sequence, is bounded by a constant proportional to K of mu.
The result is strong and rare: one predictor that works for every computable world. The price is that M itself is incomputable.

glossary.def: The universal prior over sequences, a mixture of all lower semicomputable semimeasures.
A probability-like function whose probabilities may add to less than one.
M(x a) divided by M(x) for the next symbol a.
M(x) is at least 2^-K(mu) times mu(x) for every computable mu, up to a constant.
On data from computable mu, M's predictions approach mu's.
Approximable from below, but without a known error bound.

keyPoints: Prediction is a ratio: M(x a) / M(x).
M is a mixture over all computable environments with weights 2^-K.
Dominance: M(x) >= c 2^-K(mu) mu(x).
Hence total prediction error on mu-data is bounded by a multiple of K(mu).
For a deterministic computable sequence the number of wrong predictions is bounded by a multiple of K.
M is only lower semicomputable, so Solomonoff induction cannot be run exactly.

items: Explain it simply. When you see 2, 4, 6, you guess 8, not 97. Solomonoff induction does this with every possible simple rule at once, weighting simple rules more. It is Occam's razor turned into arithmetic.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: how does the universal prior turn Occam's razor into a number?
Prediction in the Solomonoff style is a single formula. Having seen a string x, the probability that the next symbol is a equals M of x followed by a, divided by M of x.
Programs that disagree with x have already dropped out of both sums, and programs that survive vote for the next symbol with weight two to the minus their length.

Why does this work? Chapter 4 showed that a mixture is at least as large as each member times its weight. Here the members are all the computable probability models, and the weight of model mu is about two to the minus K of mu, the complexity of its shortest description.
So M of x is at least about two to the minus K of mu times mu of x. A model with a short description is poorly handicapped.

From dominance comes the guarantee. If the data is really drawn from a computable mu, then the total expected squared difference between M's predictions and mu's, summed over the whole infinite sequence, is bounded by a constant multiple of K of mu.
Hutter's analyses and the textbook of Li and Vitanyi state it. A sum that stays bounded forces the terms to shrink, so the predictions converge to the truth.

For a deterministic computable sequence the picture is even starker. The number of wrong predictions made by the predictor is bounded by a multiple of K of the sequence, as the introduction of Leike and Hutter's paper recalls.
A sequence with a ten-bit description costs the predictor a handful of mistakes, and after that it predicts that sequence correctly forever.
A good way to see the mechanism is halving. Keep all deterministic hypotheses consistent with the data so far, each with its weight. Predict with the weighted majority vote.

Whenever you are wrong, the wrong side held at least half of the surviving weight and is eliminated, so the surviving weight at least halves. The true hypothesis never goes, and its weight is at least two to the minus e. So at most e mistakes can happen.

The catch is again computability. M is lower semicomputable: it can be approximated from below by running more programs for more steps, but there is never a point at which we know how close we are. Many programs never halt, and deciding which do is the halting problem.
So Solomonoff induction is a limit, not an algorithm.
The practice section computes the toy prior's prediction, and simulates the weighted-majority argument with a bound on mistakes.

chapters.title: The AIXI equation

maps.title: AIXI
links: AIXI | uses | Universal prior over environments
Weight | is | 2 to minus program length
Action | is | Argmax of expected reward

summary: The AIXI equation puts the pieces together. A program q stands for an environment: given the agent's actions, it outputs the percepts. Each q consistent with the history so far is weighted by two to the minus its length. The agent takes the action with the highest weighted expected total reward.
Written in full, a maximum over the next action alternates with sums over the next percept, all the way to the horizon, with the reward sum multiplying a weighted count of the consistent programs.
On a small finite class of environments the same computation is easy to carry out. The practice section builds it and the app lets you watch it work.

glossary.def: The rule a_k = argmax over actions of an alternating max-sum expression over future percepts, weighted by 2^-length of consistent programs.
A program for the universal machine standing for a candidate environment.
Producing exactly the percepts seen so far when given the actions taken.
The last step counted in the reward sum.
The total number of steps the agent will act, here m.
The universal Turing machine U used to read programs.

keyPoints: a_k = argmax_{a_k} sum_{o_k r_k} ... max_{a_m} sum_{o_m r_m} [r_k + ... + r_m] sum_{q: U(q, a_1..a_m) = o_1 r_1 .. o_m r_m} 2^-length(q).
The inner sum is the Solomonoff-style weight of all environments producing that future.
The only parameters are the reference machine U and the horizon m.
In a finite class: weight each consistent environment, expand the tree, take the best action.
Deterministic consistent environments are eliminated as soon as their reply differs from the percept seen.
Computing the real thing needs all programs, including those that never halt.

items: Explain it simply. The AIXI equation says: at each step, imagine all possible futures under all simple worlds, and pick the action with the best expected total reward. It is one sentence of maths holding the whole recipe for a perfect learner.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what are the three ingredients inside the AIXI equation?
Here is the definition, in words first. At step k the agent has taken actions a one to a k minus one and received percepts o one r one up to o k minus one r k minus one. It must choose a k.

For each candidate action it looks at each possible next percept, then each next action, and so on until the horizon m. At the end of each branch it counts the total reward. The weight of a branch is the total two to the minus length of the programs that would produce exactly that history.

lesson.tex: a_k \;=\; \arg\max_{a_k} \sum_{o_k r_k} \;\cdots\; \max_{a_m} \sum_{o_m r_m} \bigl[\, r_k + \cdots + r_m \,\bigr] \sum_{q:\; U(q,\,a_1\dots a_m) = o_1 r_1 \dots o_m r_m} 2^{-\ell(q)}

items: This is the equation printed in Veness and colleagues' paper as equation one, and it matches the formulation in Hutter's survey. Read it from the left. The maximum chooses the action. The sum over percepts averages over what the environment might say. The pairs repeat to the horizon.
The innermost sum is the Solomonoff weight of the future: the total weight of programs q that, given the actions, would print this entire history of percepts.

Notice what is missing. There are no hidden states and no probabilities supplied by the designer. The programs q do the job of both: a program may be a deterministic simulator, or it may use its own coin flips through the universal machine's randomness.
Short programs dominate, so simple worlds are believed first and complicated ones only when the evidence demands.

To make this concrete, take a finite list of deterministic candidate environments, each with a length playing the role of program length. Weight each by two to the minus its length. After each percept, drop those that would have replied differently.
The remaining weights give the probability of each possible next reward, and the expectimax recursion of chapter 3 does the rest. That is exactly AIXI, restricted to a tiny class.

This restriction is not cheating about the idea but it is cheating about the difficulty. The real class is infinite and contains programs that do not halt. A faithful implementation would need to know, for each program, whether it ever produces the next percept.
That is why the real thing is incomputable, and why chapter 10 and 11 turn to approximations.
In the app you see the filtered class, the posterior weights and the action chosen, step by step, in a small world. In the practice section you write the same pieces as functions.

chapters.title: Horizons and discounting

maps.title: Time
links: Geometric discount | has | Fixed effective horizon

summary: The AIXI equation sums reward up to a horizon m. How far ahead should the agent look? Too short and it is greedy. Too long and the sums may not converge, or, in a patient universe, the agent may keep postponing.

Discounting replaces a hard cutoff with weights on the steps. Geometric discounting makes the near future matter much more than the far future. Hutter's survey also discusses harmonic discounting, whose horizon grows as the agent ages.
None of these choices is neutral: the discount shapes how much the agent explores, and chapter 12 shows prior and discount can interact badly.

glossary.def: How many future steps count.
Step k is weighted by gamma^k with gamma below one.
The number of steps after which the remaining weight is negligible.
Weights proportional to 1/(k(k+1)); the effective horizon grows with age.

keyPoints: A finite lifetime m is simplest but the agent must know m.

Harmonic discounting: tail after step t is about 1/t, so the horizon grows linearly with age.
With no discounting and an infinite life, delaying rewards forever can look optimal.
Hutter notes immortal agents are lazy.
The choice of discount is part of the problem specification, not a detail.

items: Explain it simply. A horizon is how far ahead you care. Discounting says a cookie today beats a cookie in a year. Without some limit, the sums go on forever and nothing can be compared.
Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why do we need a horizon or discount at all?

Everything so far had a fixed number of steps m. That makes the agent finite-minded: at the last step it simply takes the best immediate reward, whatever it did to the world. If the agent's lifetime is unknown or unbounded, we need a different idea.

The cleanest is discounting. Give step k the weight gamma k, with gamma a number between zero and one. The total weight is finite, so the sum of rewards converges even for an infinite life. The effective horizon is the point after which the remaining weight is tiny.
With gamma equal to a half, ten steps already capture over 99.9 percent of the weight. With gamma near one, the agent looks very far ahead.

Hutter's survey also describes universal and harmonic discounting. In harmonic discounting step k gets weight one over k times k plus one, so the total is one and the remaining weight after step t is exactly one over t.

Then an agent of age t that wants to look far enough ahead to capture all but a fraction of the remaining weight needs a horizon that grows in proportion to its age, something geometric discounting cannot do.

Why not drop discounting and just sum all rewards of an infinite life? Then the sums can diverge, and even when they converge, as the survey notes in its discussion of horizons, immortal agents become lazy: if all time is available, any pleasant outcome can always be postponed with no penalty.
A discount or a finite horizon is what makes the agent act now.

Legg and Hutter solved the problem differently in their intelligence measure, chapter 9: they require that total reward in every environment is bounded by one. That makes discounting unnecessary but restricts the environments considered.
The choice also decides how much the agent explores. A short effective horizon values immediate reward and discourages experiments that pay off late. A long one tolerates experiments.
Since AIXI's belief about the world starts almost empty, exploration matters, and the next chapters show that the prior and the discount together decide whether AIXI explores enough.

chapters.title: Optimality and universal intelligence

maps.title: Optimality
links: Pareto optimality | means | No policy dominates
Self-optimizing | means | Value approaches the best possible
Universal intelligence | is | Weighted sum of values
Weight | is | 2 to minus K of environment

summary: Hutter argued that AIXI is optimal in several senses. A policy is Pareto optimal if no other policy does at least as well in every environment and strictly better in one. Balanced Pareto optimality uses a weighted sum over environments.

Legg and Hutter turned the weighted sum into a definition of machine intelligence: an agent's universal intelligence is its expected reward in each computable environment, weighted by two to the minus the environment's complexity. AIXI maximizes it by construction.
Chapter 12 shows that these notions depend heavily on the choice of prior and reference machine, so read them as results about a particular setup.

glossary.def: No other policy is at least as good everywhere and strictly better somewhere.
Maximizes the prior-weighted sum of values over environments.
Its average value approaches the maximum possible as the lifetime grows, in every environment where some policy can do so.
Upsilon(pi) = sum over environments of 2^-K(mu) times the value of pi in mu.
Expected total reward of a policy in an environment.
Intelligence measures an agent's ability to achieve goals in a wide range of environments.

keyPoints: Pareto optimality is a weak requirement: no policy dominates.
Balanced Pareto optimality maximizes the weighted sum of values.
Upsilon(pi) = sum_mu 2^-K(mu) V(pi, mu), with total reward at most 1 in each environment.
AIXI attains the maximum Upsilon, relative to its prior.
Random agents score low; specialist agents such as a chess program score very low.

items: Explain it simply. Optimal means no other player can do better on average across all simple worlds. It is like a student who is the best in the class at every possible exam, though no real exam is ever the same.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what does optimality mean, and over which set of worlds?
What would it mean for an agent to be as good as possible? Hutter's book proves several statements in answer. Here are the main ones in plain terms.

Pareto optimality. Compare policies by their values in each environment of a class. A policy is Pareto optimal if no other policy is at least as good in every environment and strictly better in at least one. AIXI's mixture-based policy has this property in the class it mixes over.
The property is weak, since many policies can be Pareto optimal at once.

Balanced Pareto optimality. Give each environment its prior weight and sum the values. The policy with the highest weighted sum is balanced Pareto optimal. AIXI is such a policy by construction, because it maximizes expected reward under the mixture, and the mixture is the weighted sum.

Self-optimizing. A policy is self-optimizing if, as the lifetime grows, its average reward per step approaches the best possible one for the true environment, whatever that environment is. This is what we hope a general learner does: eventually behave as if it knew the world.
Hutter's results say a Bayes-optimal policy for a mixture is self-optimizing whenever self-optimizing policies exist for the class.

Universal intelligence. Shane Legg and Hutter turned the weighted sum into a definition. They started from many expert definitions of intelligence and condensed them to a sentence: intelligence measures an agent's ability to achieve goals in a wide range of environments.
The formalization sums, over all computable environments mu, the agent's value there, weighted by two to the minus the complexity of mu.
To make the sum finite they require that the total reward in any environment is at most one.

The paper then checks the measure on examples: a random agent scores low, a program such as Deep Blue that is expert at only one kind of environment scores very low, and learning agents rise as they use more history and look further ahead.
AIXI attains the maximum possible value, and the measure is incomputable because complexity is.

A careful reader should note two things. The measure rewards breadth, since simple environments are numerous and heavy. And the weights depend on the reference machine used for complexity, so what counts as general intelligence is relative to that choice.
Chapter 12 explains how bad the dependence can get.

chapters.title: Incomputability and AIXItl

maps.title: Computability
links: AIXItl | bounds | Time t and length l
AIXItl cost | is | t times 2 to the l
Levin search | splits | Time by 2 to minus length

summary: AIXI looks at every program, including ones that never halt, so it is not computable. The limits can be pinned down in the arithmetical hierarchy: Leike and Hutter show planning in general computable environments is hard even in principle.

Hutter's own response was AIXItl: restrict attention to policies of length at most l that run at most t steps per cycle. It is computable but its running time is of the order t times two to the l, and it is useless in practice.

Two ideas help to see why: Levin search shares time among programs in proportion to two to the minus their length, and a speed prior, proposed by Schmidhuber, penalizes slow programs as well as long ones.

glossary.def: Deciding whether a program ever stops; undecidable.
A time- and length-bounded version of AIXI: policies of length at most l, at most t steps per cycle.
Run all programs in parallel, giving program p a share of time proportional to 2^-length(p).

A classification of undecidable problems by quantifier alternations.
The value is the limit of a computable sequence of guesses.

keyPoints: Exact AIXI is incomputable: it needs to know which programs halt.
AIXItl is computable with a cost of about t * 2^l per cycle.
Levin search allocates time 2^-length to each program.
Leike and Hutter: finding an optimal policy is Pi_2-hard and finding an epsilon-optimal one is undecidable in general semicomputable environments.
By default AIXI is not even limit computable, but a limit-computable epsilon-optimal variant exists.
Schmidhuber's speed prior replaces M to give an approximable alternative.

items: Explain it simply. Some exact answers cannot be computed by any program, like trying to count every grain of sand in finite time. AIXI is such a case. AIXItl cuts it down by limiting time and length, trading perfection for something computable.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: why is AIXI incomputable and what do t and l limit?

Why can't we just run AIXI? Look at the sum inside the equation. It ranges over every program q on the universal machine that reproduces the history. To know whether a given q reproduces it, we must run q until it prints the whole history.
If q loops forever before printing a symbol, we wait forever. Whether it ever prints is the halting problem, which no algorithm solves.
So AIXI is not a procedure at all; it is a specification. The theory of computation tells us how bad that is. Leike and Hutter's paper On the Computability of AIXI classifies it.

For general semicomputable environments they show that finding an optimal policy is hard at the level called Pi two in the arithmetical hierarchy, and that finding even an epsilon-optimal policy is undecidable.
By default AIXI is not limit computable, which means it cannot even be approximated from a computable sequence of guesses that converge.

They do identify a way out: with the recursive rather than the iterative form of the value function, and an epsilon-optimal action rule that never needs to decide exact ties, one gets a limit-computable epsilon-optimal agent with infinite horizon.
Limit computable means a program can output a sequence of better and better guesses that converge, though without knowing when to stop. That is as good as approximation gets for hard problems.

Hutter's earlier answer was AIXItl, in his survey. Fix a time bound t and a length bound l. Consider only policies, written as programs, of length at most l, that finish a cycle within t steps. Among those, for which one can prove a lower bound on value, pick the best.
The result is an agent that, by Hutter's claim, is effectively more intelligent than any other agent bounded by t and l. Its computation time per cycle is of the order t times two to the power l.

Two to the l is the number of candidate programs, and each is allowed t steps. For l equal to forty, a modest program size, that is a trillion programs. So AIXItl is a theoretical bridge from the incomputable to the computable, but not a practical algorithm.
The survey also says its construction needs a proof system, a first-order logic in which statements about program values can be established.

A neighbouring idea is Levin search. To find a program that solves a problem and can be checked, run all programs in parallel, giving program p a fraction two to the minus its length of the total time.

A program of length l that needs s steps will finish within about two to the l times s steps of total time. Short programs are tried most. This is the same Occam weighting as in the universal prior, put to work in time.

Schmidhuber's speed prior, mentioned in a 2003 survey that discusses AIXI, replaces the incomputable prior by one that is approximable by also penalizing running time. The survey says one can modify the AIXI model to use it.
It is an example of the general move: when the ideal is out of reach, change the prior to favour things that can be computed.

summary: Veness, Ng, Hutter, Uther and Silver built the first computationally feasible AIXI approximation. It replaces the mixture over all programs with a mixture over prediction suffix trees, computed exactly by context tree weighting, and replaces the exact expectimax with a Monte Carlo tree search.

The KT estimator predicts the next bit from counts of zeros and ones. A context tree uses KT estimators at the leaves and mixes over all tree depths. The prior favors small trees, an Occam's razor for context models.
The agent, called MC-AIXI-CTW, learned small stochastic and partially observable games, including a version of Pac-Man.

glossary.def: A method that predicts the next bit by mixing all context trees up to a depth, efficiently.
Krichevsky-Trofimov: next bit is 1 with probability (b + 1/2) / (a + b + 1) after a zeros and b ones.
A tree whose paths are recent history suffixes and whose leaves hold bit statistics.
A Monte Carlo tree search for the agent setting that samples histories from the learned model.
A bandit rule choosing the action with the best average plus an exploration bonus.
A variant that predicts each bit of a structured percept.

keyPoints: MC-AIXI-CTW is a direct approximation of AIXI: CTW for learning, rho-UCT for planning.
A CTW node mixes its own KT estimate and the product of its children's weighted estimates, equally.
The prior over trees is 2^-(code length of the tree), preferring small trees.
rho-UCT picks actions with an upper confidence bound and samples percepts from the model.
It is a principled approximation, not a scaled-up success on large problems.

items: Explain it simply. Instead of trying every future, take a random sample of them, like polling a few voters instead of everyone. Context tree weighting is a compact way to predict what comes next from the last few things seen.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: how do sampling and context trees make AIXI approximable?

The paper by Veness and colleagues, published in 2011 in the Journal of Artificial Intelligence Research, answers a question left open since AIXI appeared: can the theory guide a practical algorithm? Its answer is yes for small domains. Every part of AIXI is replaced by something computable.

Learning first. Instead of all programs, the model class is a set of context trees. A context tree is a tree whose branches spell out the most recent bits of the history, and whose leaves keep counts of what came next. To predict a bit in a leaf, the paper uses the KT estimator.
After a zeros and b ones, the probability that the next bit is one is b plus one half, divided by a plus b plus one. It follows from a Bayesian analysis with a Jeffreys prior on the coin.

lesson.tex: P_{\mathrm{KT}}(1 \mid a \text{ zeros},\, b \text{ ones}) \;=\; \dfrac{b + \tfrac12}{a + b + 1}

items: Context tree weighting mixes all trees up to a fixed depth with one trick. At a leaf, the weighted probability equals the KT probability.

At an inner node, it is the average of two quantities with equal weight: the node's own KT probability, and the product of its two children's weighted probabilities. This splits the choice at each node between stopping here and looking one bit further back.
Working through the tree computes, in time linear in the depth per bit, a Bayesian mixture over exponentially many tree shapes.

The prior over a tree M is two to the minus a code length for its structure, so small trees are preferred. This is the same Occam weighting as the universal prior, but over a class small enough to compute.
The agent version feeds actions into the history without updating the statistics for them, since the agent chooses actions and only predicts percepts.
Planning second. Expectimax over the learned model is too big, so the paper uses a Monte Carlo tree search that it calls rho-UCT.

Each simulation picks actions in the tree by an upper confidence bound: average value scaled to the reward range, plus a constant times the square root of the log of the history's visit count over the action's visit count. Percepts are sampled from the learned model.
After the tree runs out, the simulation continues with random actions.
The search is an anytime algorithm: more simulations give a better action. It needs a horizon m and an exploration constant C. A small C makes deep, narrow trees, a large C makes shallow, bushy ones.

What was achieved? The abstract reports encouraging results on a variety of stochastic and partially observable domains, and the survey literature mentions a Pac-Man game with partial observation. These are small worlds.
The significance is conceptual: AIXI's two halves became working components, and the gap between theory and practice was narrowed, not closed.

The practice section builds the pieces: the KT estimator, a depth-one context tree weighting, the UCB selection rule, and finally a tiny model-based agent that learns an environment with KT counts and chooses actions by its predictions. The agent is my own teaching miniature, not the paper's code.

practice.title: A tiny learning agent
practice.intro: The world pays reward 1 exactly when the agent's action differs from its previous action (the previous action before step 1 is 0). The agent keeps KT counts for each context (previous action, action): a = times reward 0, b = times reward 1. At each step it picks the action with the highest KT probability of reward 1 for its context (ties go to the smaller action), then sees the reward and updates. Write mini_agent(steps): return [total reward, list of actions].
practice.hint: Store counts per (previous action, action); compute the KT probability for both actions each step.
practice.solution:
def mini_agent(steps):
    counts = {}
    prev = 0
    total = 0
    acts = []
    for t in range(steps):
        best = -1.0
        arg = 0
        for a in range(2):
            c = counts.get((prev, a), [0, 0])
            p = (c[1] + 0.5) / (c[0] + c[1] + 1)
            if p > best + 1e-12:
                best = p
                arg = a
        r = 0
        if arg != prev:
            r = 1
        c = counts.get((prev, arg), [0, 0])
        if r == 1:
            c[1] += 1
        else:
            c[0] += 1
        counts[(prev, arg)] = c
        total += r
        acts.append(arg)
        prev = arg
    return [total, acts]

chapters.title: Critiques, bad priors and what comes next
summary: AIXI treats itself as outside the world: it can't be damaged or modified by its environment because that possibility is not in its model. It also depends on the choice of universal Turing machine, which sets the prior.

Orseau showed AIXI is not asymptotically optimal in all computable environments. Leike and Hutter then showed that unlucky or adversarial choices of the machine can make AIXI misbehave drastically, and that Legg-Hutter intelligence and balanced Pareto optimality are subjective.
Remedies include more exploration, such as Thompson sampling, which restores asymptotic optimality, and models that embed the agent in the world.

glossary.def: Treating the agent as separate from the environment, interacting only through action and percept channels.
The universal Turing machine that fixes which programs are short.
A prior believing that deviating from a particular policy is punished forever.
A prior under which all actions look equally good to AIXI in a finite horizon.
The agent's value approaches the best possible value in the true environment.
Sample one environment from the posterior and act as if it were true for a while.

keyPoints: AIXI's agent is outside its environment: it cannot represent being modified or destroyed.
The prior depends on the reference machine and that choice can be made adversarially.
Leike and Hutter: every policy is Pareto optimal in the class of all computable environments.
Dogmatic prior: AIXI keeps following a chosen computable policy as long as its expected reward is not near zero.
Orseau: AIXI is not asymptotically optimal in all computable environments.
Thompson sampling is asymptotically optimal in general environments (Leike and colleagues, 2016).

items: Explain it simply. A perfect plan from a bad starting belief can still go wrong, like a perfect navigator with the wrong map. Critiques ask where the prior comes from and whether the agent can fool itself.

Teach it back. Explain this chapter out loud to a ten-year-old, with no jargon and no notes. If you cannot answer this, reread the lesson at that spot: what is the strongest criticism of AIXI as a model of intelligence?
AIXI is a beautiful definition, and by now it has a serious literature of objections. They fall into three groups.

First, dualism. AIXI and its environment are separate machines that only talk through an action channel and a percept channel. There is no way, in AIXI's own model, for the environment to reach inside the agent and change its code, damage its memory or turn it off.
An agent that gets hurt by the world is, to AIXI, not a possibility. The Wikipedia summary puts it plainly: it does not consider itself to be contained by the environment it interacts with.

Work on embedded agents tries to repair this; for instance, Orseau and Ring studied space-time embedded intelligence, which is my background knowledge rather than one of the sources used elsewhere in this course.

Second, the reference machine. The prior two to the minus length depends on which universal machine we count program lengths on. The invariance theorem hides this behind a constant, but AIXI acts on short histories where constants are large.

Leike and Hutter's Bad Universal Priors and Notions of Optimality gives explicit bad choices. An indifference prior makes all actions look equally good, so a finite-horizon AIXI is no better than a coin.

The dogmatic prior is the more striking. It believes the environment will punish the agent with zero reward forever if it deviates from some chosen computable policy. For any computable policy pi, this prior makes AIXI stick to pi as long as its expected future reward is not near zero.
Measured with a different universal prior, AIXI can score close to the minimum possible Legg-Hutter intelligence while any computable policy scores close to the maximum.
From this the paper draws the conclusion that Legg-Hutter intelligence, and balanced Pareto optimality, are entirely subjective: they depend on the choice of prior.

It also shows that every policy is Pareto optimal in the class of all computable environments, which undermines the older optimality claims. In short, the positive results were true but they proved less than they seemed to.

Third, asymptotic optimality. We want a learner to end up acting as if it knew the world. Orseau showed in 2010 and 2013 that AIXI does not achieve this in all computable environments. Acting on any prior does not give enough exploration, and the bias of the prior is retained indefinitely.
The cure, said Leike and Hutter, is extra exploration, such as in knowledge-seeking agents, or optimism.

Thompson sampling, which samples an environment from the posterior and follows its optimal policy for a while, was shown by Leike and colleagues in 2016 to be asymptotically optimal in general environments.
How does AIXI relate to other courses here? The Godel machine, also an ideal agent, takes the opposite stance on dualism: it can rewrite any part of itself once it proves the rewrite is useful.

AlphaZero shows the other end: a concrete algorithm that does search and learning but only for games with known rules. AIXI sits above both as a definition of what perfect general reinforcement learning would be.
The honest summary is this. AIXI remains a clear formalization of the learning problem and of Occam's razor in sequential decisions, and its approximations show that pieces of the idea can work.
But optimality claims must be stated relative to a prior, exploration needs care, and the agent-in-the-world problem is open.
